food.text: The Trans-Caspian Railway, begun in 1879 and reaching Samarkand by 1888, let merchants import sugar, kerosene, wood and iron into Central Asia while cotton exports soared from 873,092 pudy in 1888 to 3,588,025 pudy by 1893. Merchant N. I. Reshetnikov even offered private funds to push the line further, hoping to expand this booming trade.

Kumis, a fermented drink made from mare's milk, stayed central to the diet of Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Bashkirs, Kalmyks and Mongols across the steppe. Because mare's milk holds more sugar than cow's or goat's milk, fermented kumis reached a mild alcohol content of only 0.7 to 2.5 percent.

Central Asian cuisine mixed Persian, Turkic, Mongol and Chinese traditions, further reshaped by the arrival of Uyghur, Slav, Korean, Tatar, Dungan and German settlers. Cooks used scarce fuel such as poplar wood, saxaul shrubs and dried animal dung to heat tandyr ovens for baking flatbread, samsa pastries and meats.

Governor-General Nikolai Rozenbakh pointed to the rising trade in imported sugar and other goods to argue for extending the Trans-Caspian Railway toward Tashkent. The line had stalled at Samarkand for ten years before finally reaching Tashkent and Andijan in 1898.

A typical meal began with tea or fresh tandyr nan bread, followed by a soup called shorpo or pulled noodles called lagman, then a main course of pilov made with rice, meat and carrots. Guests might next be offered dumplings or grilled meat skewers, with fresh fruit standing in for dessert, all laid out on a floor cloth called a dastarkhan.

Central Asian nomads reportedly used freeze distillation to strengthen kumis, which was only mildly alcoholic on its own. The fermented mare's milk could also be distilled further into a stronger spirit called arkhi.

Because mare's milk stayed a limited commodity, industrial-scale kumis production relied instead on cow's milk, which is richer in fat and protein but lower in lactose. Producers fortified this cow's milk with added sucrose or with modified whey to imitate the composition of true mare's milk.

Besh barmak, a lamb dish eaten with the hands, and horse meat were foods found mainly among Kazakhs and Kyrgyz rather than across the whole region. This reflected a divide between the nomadic, meat-and-dairy diet of Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan and the grain-based cooking of settled oasis towns elsewhere.

art.text: Central Asia fell largely under the control of Russia in the 19th century. Russian Turkestan (1867–1917) was administered as a krai or governor-generalship. As a consequence of Russian colonization, European fine arts, meaning painting, sculpture and graphics, developed in Central Asia.

The temple of Avalokiteshvara was built from 1911 to 1913 as a symbol of the new, independent Bogdo Khanate of Mongolia. Its statue, believed to open the eyes of wisdom in sentient beings, symbolised the Mongolian people's step into modern civilisation.
Mongolian temple building in the renaissance tradition continued into the 18th, 19th and early 20th centuries. Mongolian architects also used translations of the Kangyur as a resource for their work.
In Bukhara, the Chor Minor (Char Minar) was completed in 1807. It served as the gateway to a madrasa and has an unusual design: a tetrapylon crowned by four heavy circular corner towers.

The Choijin Lama Süm temple was built in 1904 and is now a museum. The Mongolian artist and art historian N. Chultem identified three styles of traditional Mongolian architecture: Mongolian, Tibetan and Chinese. This temple is an example of one built in the Chinese tradition.
Agvaanhaidav (1779–1838) was a Mongolian writer who described the process of building a Maitreya temple. His work belongs to the tradition of temple building that continued into the 19th century.
Agvaanceren (1785–1849) wrote Aahar shaahar, a work titled Building and Repairing Temples. It is one of the written guides on temple construction from Mongolia's 19th century.

war.text: During the 19th century, the Imperial Russian Army succeeded in conquering all of Central Asia. Most of the land became known as Russian Turkestan, named for the Turkic peoples who made up the vast majority of its population. Alarmed by Russia's gains, the British Empire sought to reinforce India, which triggered the Great Game.

After General Cherniaev took Tashkent in 1865, Khodjend, Djizak and Samarkand fell to the Russians in quick succession over the next three years. The Khanate of Kokand and the Emirate of Bukhara were repeatedly defeated. In 1867 the governor-generalship of Russian Turkestan was established, headquartered at Tashkent.

On 2 February 1913, the Bogd Khanate of Mongolia sent cavalry to "liberate" Inner Mongolia from China. About 10,000 Khalkha and Inner Mongolian cavalry (about 3,500 of them Inner Mongols) defeated 70,000 Chinese soldiers and controlled almost all of Inner Mongolia. The war killed 400 Mongol soldiers and 3,795 Chinese soldiers. The Mongolian army retreated in 1914 for lack of weapons.

The Transcaspian region was annexed in 1881 to 1885 in a campaign led by Generals Mikhail Annenkov and Mikhail Skobelev. Ashgabat was taken from Persia, while Merv and Panjdeh came under Russian control, with Panjdeh taken from Afghanistan.
The Russians built forts east from the Aral Sea between 1847 and 1853. The later Russian capture of Tashkent in 1865 and Samarkand in 1868 produced no British response.

In 1839 Perovsky's attack on Khiva failed. That same year Abbot went to Khiva to negotiate the release of Russian slaves held there, hoping to remove a pretext for invasion, but he failed. The next year Richmond Shakespear succeeded and led 416 Russian slaves to the Caspian. Perovsky's expedition had lost its camels by the thousands in the winter cold, and 1,054 soldiers died during it.
Charles Stoddart went to Bokhara in 1838 and was arrested. Arthur Conolly went in 1841 to secure his release, but both men were executed in 1842.

Russia also annexed the Chu and Ili Valleys and the city of Kuldja from the Chinese Empire. After Yakub Beg died at Korla in 1877, his state collapsed as China reconquered the area. Russia returned Kuldja to Beijing in 1884 after lengthy negotiations.

Russia refused to sell weapons to the Bogd Khanate, and Tsar Nicholas II called its campaign "Mongolian imperialism". The United Kingdom urged Russia to abolish Mongolian independence, fearing that if Mongolians gained independence, Central Asians would revolt.

Some Russian officials cited the Dungan Revolt in the neighboring Qing Empire as proof of the threat of Islam and advocated religious repression in newly conquered territories. General Kaufman and his superior Dmitry Milyutin preferred mild religious tolerance instead.

literature.text: The roots of Central Asian studies go back to the 19th century Anglo-Russian Great Game. British and Russian agents, soldiers and scholars travelled the region, and Central Asia became a subject of systematic information collection. The British Royal Geographical Society and Russian Geographical Society published dozens of travel books on the region.

For centuries Western European literature and cartography used "Tartary" as a blanket term for a vast part of Asia, bounded by the Caspian Sea, the Ural Mountains and the Pacific Ocean. The name was in active use from the 13th to the 19th centuries, but by the mid-19th century its use for Siberia and Central Asia had waned.
The Ukrainian poet Taras Shevchenko (1814-1861) was assigned to the area of Aktau on military work. From 1964 to 1991 the city, by then grown, bore the name "Shevchenko" in his honour.

Travellers' memoirs are among the oldest sources for Central Asia, and some of the earliest were left by Arab geographers. In the 19th century numerous Europeans and Americans published their own travelogues of the region.

The Journal of the Central Asian Society began publication in 1914. It was titled the Journal of the Royal Central Asian Society from 1931 to 1969, when it became Asian Affairs and its focus shifted from Central Asia to South Asia and East Asia.

science.text: Until the 19th century, European knowledge of inner Asia remained extremely scarce and fragmentary, and mapmakers labelled it Tartary. The voyages of Egor Meyendorff and Alexander von Humboldt into the region gave rise to the term Central Asia in the early 19th century.

During the 19th century, Central Asia became a subject of systematical information collection and organization. This was thanks to numerous travels by British and Russian agents, soldiers and scholars during the Anglo-Russian Great Game. The roots of Central Asian studies as a discipline go back to this effort.
In 1897 the railway reached Tashkent. In 1906 a direct rail link with European Russia was opened across the steppe from Orenburg to Tashkent, tying Turkestan much more closely to European Russia.

Egor Meyendorff's and Alexander von Humboldt's voyages into the region gave rise to the term Central Asia in the early 19th century, along with supplementary terms such as Inner Asia. Russian eastward expansionism meanwhile led to the term "Siberia" being coined for the Asian half of the Russian Empire.

Russian eastward expansionism led to the term Siberia being coined for the Asian half of the Russian Empire. By the mid-19th century, the old European use of Tartary as a term for Siberia and Central Asia had waned.

The British Royal Geographical Society and the Russian Geographical Society published dozens of travel books on Central Asia. These books helped turn the accounts of agents, soldiers and scholars into organized knowledge of the region.

politics.text: Between 1847 and 1853 Russia built forts eastward from the Aral Sea. Its capture of Tashkent in 1865 and Samarkand in 1868 produced no British response, even as Britain worried about defending India.

The Great Game began in 1838, when Britain decided to make the Emirate of Afghanistan a protectorate. It also planned to use the Ottoman Empire, Qajar Iran, the Khanate of Khiva and the Emirate of Bukhara as buffer states between the two empires. The final result was a neutral zone in the middle of Afghanistan.

Borjigin nobles proclaimed Mongolia's independence in 1911 and established the Bogd Khanate. This came after their political authority had declined under Qing rule, which had annexed the Khalkha khanates in 1691.
Between 1801 and 1914, an estimated 7 million settlers moved from European Russia to Siberia. About 85 percent of them arrived during the quarter-century before World War I.

In 1866 the Dungans captured Kulja and massacred its inhabitants. In June 1871 General Kolpakovsky crossed the border and occupied the city (4 July 1871). The Russian Foreign Office told China the province would be returned as soon as the Emperor could send enough troops to maintain order.

After Russian conquests in the 1860s and 1870s, western Central Asia became a Governor-Generalship led by Konstantin von Kaufman. Russian authorities debated whether to repress Islam or tolerate it. Kaufman and his superior Dmitry Milyutin preferred mild tolerance, though Kaufman worried about pan-Islam movements.

The railway reached Tashkent in 1897, and a direct link with European Russia across the steppe from Orenburg opened in 1906. A Migration Department in St. Petersburg oversaw the flow of Slavic settlers into Turkestan. They took scarce land and water from the Kyrgyz, Kazakhs and Sarts.

China regained control of Chinese Turkestan in 1877 and asked for Kulja back. A treaty concluded at Livadia in 1879 was rejected by the Chinese government, and the more favorable Treaty of Saint Petersburg (1881) replaced it. Russia left Kulja in 1883, one of the few Chinese successes against a Western power in the nineteenth century.

Some Russian officials cited the Dungan Revolt in the neighboring Qing Empire as proof that Islam was a potential threat. They argued for a policy of religious repression in the newly conquered territories.

In 1916 a decree conscripting natives into labour battalions, who had previously been exempt from military service, sparked the Basmachi Revolt. Thousands of settlers were killed, and the Kazakhs attacked Russian and Cossack villages, killing indiscriminately. The Russians' revenge was merciless, and a military force drove 300,000 Kazakhs to flee into the mountains or to China. When approximately 80,000 of them returned the next year, many were slaughtered by Tsarist forces.

Once the railway from Orenburg to Tashkent was open, much larger numbers of Slavic settlers flowed into Turkestan than before. Their settlement was overseen by a specially created Migration Department in St. Petersburg.
Rudyard Kipling's 1901 novel Kim made the term "Great Game" popular. It also gave the phrase a new implication of great power rivalry.
Maqsud Shah, Khan of Kumul from 1908 to 1930, was described as one of the last ruling Chinggisids. His rule shows how descendants of Genghis Khan held power into the twentieth century.

philosophy.text: By 1914, the Buryats of southeastern Siberia had built 48 Buddhist monasteries called datsans. This growth made Buddhism a central force in shaping Buryat culture during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

The Jadid movement arose among Muslims in Russian Central Asia in the late 19th and early 20th century. Its members believed that moral and societal decay could only be reversed through a revival of pure Islamic belief combined with modern, European-style education.

By the 1820s, nearly all Yakuts in Siberia claimed to have converted to the Russian Orthodox Church. At the same time, they kept practicing traditional tengri beliefs alongside their new Christian faith.
The Naqshbandi Sufi order traced its roots to Bukhara in Central Asia. In the 19th century it spearheaded Muslim resistance to Russian expansion into the region.

Crimean Tatar educator Ismail Gasprinsky, who lived from 1851 to 1914, led the push to reform Islamic schooling with modern methods. His ideas were carried into Central Asia by intellectuals such as Mahmud Khoja Behbudiy, who founded one of Turkestan's first Jadid schools.

Throughout the 19th and early 20th century, Russian scholars studied Tibetan Buddhism as it spread through Siberia. Many of these scholars, often with Christian missionary backgrounds, dismissed Siberian Buddhism as a backward, defective faith.
In Buryat Buddhism, the chief lama held the title Pandit Hambo Lama, meaning learned prior. Starting in 1809, this leadership passed from the Tsongol Datsan to the priors of the Tamchinsky Datsan.

In 1869, the Mongolian lama Choi-Manramba began teaching Indo-Tibetan medicine at the Tsugol Datsan in Buryatia. From there, this blend of Buddhist learning and healing knowledge spread to other Buryat monasteries.
In 1878, the Duynhor Kalachakra School was founded at the Aga Datsan in Buryatia. This completed the establishment of Tibetan-style schools for higher spiritual education in the region.
By 1914, a bookstore in Samarqand catering to Jadid reformers sold books in Tatar, Ottoman, Arabic and Persian. Its stock covered history, geography, general science, medicine and religion.
By 1887, twenty-nine Buddhist print shops were operating in Buryatia. Together they published about 2,000 book titles written in Tibetan and Mongolian before being destroyed in the 1930s.

culture.text: From the 13th to the 19th centuries, Western European writers and mapmakers used the name Tartary for a vast part of Asia reaching from the Caspian Sea and Ural Mountains to the Pacific Ocean. The name had no connection with the real polities or ethnic groups of the region, and until the 19th century European knowledge of the area remained scarce and fragmentary.

Until the 1870s, Russian interference in Central Asia was mostly minimal, leaving native ways of life intact and local government structures in place. After the conquest of Turkestan following 1865, the Russians gradually took large parts of the steppe and gave the land to Russian farmers.

The explorers Egor Meyendorff and Alexander von Humboldt made voyages into the region in the early 19th century, which gave rise to the term Central Asia. Russian eastward expansion led to the term Siberia being coined for the Asian half of the Russian Empire, and by the mid-19th century Tartary had waned as a name.

In the 19th century, Central Asia became a subject of systematic information collection thanks to travels by British and Russian agents, soldiers and scholars during the Anglo-Russian Great Game. The British Royal Geographical Society and the Russian Geographical Society published dozens of travel books on the region.

In 1897 the railway reached Tashkent, and in 1906 a direct rail link with European Russia opened across the steppe from Orenburg to Tashkent. Many more Slavic settlers arrived, overseen by a Migration Department in St. Petersburg. Kyrgyz, Kazakhs and Sarts resented the newcomers for taking scarce land and water.

The late 19th century Russian Orientalist Vasilii Vladimirovich Bartold is credited as the founder of the modern study of Central Asian history. His work came during the same era that saw the Anglo-Russian Great Game spur British and Russian scholarship on the region.
